newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-"Dances with Wolves" author buries hatchet with Custer.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-"Dances with Wolves" author buries hatchet with Custer.

text.p: Help is coming for Gen. George Custer and his battered reputation from an unlikely ally.

Hero or villain, dashing soldier or glory-seeking fool, Custer remains a controversial figure 120 years after he led 210 7th Cavalry troopers to death at the hands of the Sioux at the Little Big Horn. These days he is usually seen as a symbol of the cruel treatment of Indians by the United States.
But author Michael Blake, who eulogised the Indians in his novel and Oscar-winning film "Dances with Wolves," shows Custer in a sympathetic light in his new book, "Marching to Valhalla."
"I used to be politically correct. Now I'm politically incorrect," Blake joked in an interview with Reuters.
The book is written in the form of a campaign journal as Custer marches across the Great Plains to his fate. "I began reading about him and became fascinated by him," Blake said.

"I didn't want to revise Custer but to portray him as a thinking, feeling person. He was an extraordinary man. Most people now think of him as a jerk, an idiot and an egomaniac. In my view he knew and respected Native Americans more than most people of his era. That's not to say he wasn't a racist. Everyone was then -- it was taken for granted," he said.
"He's a fall guy for political incorrectness of the last century. Yes, he killed Indians, but he did what he perceived to be his duty carrying out the policy of the government."

Blake has even taken to dressing up as Custer. He donned the blue 7th Cavalry uniform for a book reading at a Fort Lauderdale public library recently and acted the part of the general as he sat writing at his desk while on the campaign.

Custer mused aloud about his fears that his military career was being ruined by politicians, his love of soldiering and life in the field, and his devotion to his wife, Libbie. He looked forward to engaging his enemy, unaware of the way in which he was fated to earn immortality.

Asked about the enduring interest in Custer, Blake said: "He was a rebel his whole life. He was unconventional. His superiors admired his fighting ability but found him too exotic." He also said Custer, even though he is chiefly remembered for a disaster, was a tremendous soldier. He was the youngest Union general in the Civil War, where he gained a reputation as a fearless cavalry commander.
"He made no mistakes at the Little Big Horn. Having been discovered, he had no choice but to attack."

Custer's decision to split his command as they charged into the Indian camp, much criticised by many military scholars, had proven to be a sucessful tactic before, he said. "The power of the Indians simply ran over him. They had never before been that united and they never were again."

Blake is working on a movie screenplay for "Marching to Valhalla" due next month. Hollywood heart-throb Brad Pitt is slated to play Custer -- the latest of many screen portrayals -- and production should begin next summer.

Blake's own favourite screen Custer is Errol Flynn, who played him in "They Died with Their Boots On." Although the film was wildly inaccurate historically, Flynn captured Custer's jaunty, flamboyant side. No other portrayal has come close, he said, particularly not Richard Mulligan's in "Little Big Man" in which Custer was played as a drunken buffoon.

"Dances with Wolves," directed by and starring his friend Kevin Costner, won a fistful of Oscars including a best screenplay award for Blake. The movie depicted the Indians in a glowing light as noble savages, the whites as drunks, predators and killers.
The Custer book had annoyed many of his old fans, he said. "A lot of Indian people are up in arms -- white people too. They can't believe I'm doing this. I like Custer and it shows."
